item.title: Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.19414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce FormCraft, a framework for representing acquired operations as first-class capabilities that can be recursively composed, directly invoked, and selectively retained in a persistent library through domain-specific verification. The framework separates capability well-formedness and public callability from later admission to persistent storage while preserving formation provenance and operational identity. We formalize recursive compositional closure over a uniform capability space and show that formed composites can be reused through the same public interface without re-forming their historical derivation. Experiments across continuous, discrete, propositional, and sequence domains demonstrate instance-independent reuse, independent checking, persistent acquisition, and reduced reuse-time search work under first-class exposure.
item.dc:creator: Hang Lin

item.title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
item.description: arXiv:2610.19764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.
item.dc:creator: Seulkee Baek

item.title: Typechecking without Minimum Types: Finite Bases and Backward Checking for $F_{<:}^{\top}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.20356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System $F_{<:}^{\top}$ has decidable subtyping but lacks minimum types. We prove that typechecking is decidable for arbitrary explicitly annotated terms with unrestricted subsumption. The difficulty is that type abstraction uses a variable's declared bound to type its body, while quantified subtyping forgets that bound. We construct finite covers that preserve all required subtype comparisons across this change of context. These covers yield a compositional finite typing basis and a decision procedure. We then derive a backward checker that propagates acceptable targets without constructing the complete typing basis. Rectangularity of typing families gives a uniform elimination domain while retaining every result type, even when the canonical type is not least. Finite inverse families transport targets through type substitution. The same inverse specification recovers bound forgetting and yields finite type-avoidance families. Both typechecking procedures are total Rocq functions proved equivalent to the original typing judgment. For a separate symbolic word-RAM realization, we prove a quartic worst-case work bound. We measure family representation sizes and comparison storage in independent OCaml prototypes on synthetic checking judgments.
item.dc:creator: Mingkun Xiao, Yixuan Sun

item.title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.19238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.
item.dc:creator: Casper L. Christensen, Kyle J. Ray, Dmitry Manning-Coe, Adam Shai, Paul Riechers

item.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.20459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.
item.dc:creator: Jiatong Li, Yatao Bian

item.title: Open-Source AI-Powered Optimization in Scalene: Advancing Python Performance Profiling with DeepSeek-R1 and LLaMA 3.2
item.description: arXiv:2502.10299v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Python's flexibility and ease of use come at the cost of performance inefficiencies, requiring developers to rely on profilers to optimize execution. SCALENE, a high-performance CPU, GPU, and memory profiler, provides fine-grained insights into Python applications while running significantly faster than traditional profilers. Originally, SCALENE integrated OpenAI's API to generate AI-powered optimization suggestions, but its reliance on a proprietary API limited accessibility. This study explores the feasibility of using opensource large language models (LLMs), such as DeepSeek-R1 and Llama 3.2, to generate optimization recommendations within SCALENE. Our evaluation reveals that DeepSeek-R1 provides effective code optimizations comparable to proprietary models. We integrate DeepSeek-R1 into SCALENE to automatically analyze performance bottlenecks and suggest improvements, enhancing SCALENE's utility while maintaining its open-source nature. This study demonstrates that open-source LLMs can be viable alternatives for AI-driven code optimization, paving the way for more accessible and cost-effective performance analysis tools.
item.dc:creator: Saem Hasan, Sanju Basak

item.title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
item.description: arXiv:2603.22519v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks. This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting. We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hind, Basel Shbita, Bo Wu, Farhan Ahmed, Chad DeLuca, Nathan Fulton, David Cox, Dan Gutfreund

item.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
item.description: arXiv:2604.02598v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed or stepped through. We argue that grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension with explorable theorems, a system that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging each step. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on that example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study ($n = 16$) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-reading task, participants who had access to the provided explorability features gave better, more correct, and more detailed answers to comprehension questions, demonstrating a stronger overall understanding of the underlying mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Hita Kambhamettu, Will Crichton, Sean Welleck, Harrison Goldstein, Andrew Head

item.title: Cover Semantics for Intuitionistic Modalities
item.description: arXiv:2607.11352v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intuitionistic modal logic (IML) has inspired several developments in programming languages including modal type systems for staging, computational effects and language-based security. IMLs are typically studied using Kripke-style relational semantics, which simplifies proofs of meta-theoretic properties, such as completeness and consistency, by making it easy to construct models. Kripke-style relational semantics, however, relies upon classical reasoning principles, which makes it unappealing from a computational perspective and unsuitable for formalization in a constructive type theory. Goldblatt provides an alternative semantics for IMLs by extending Beth-Kripke-Joyal-style "cover" semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic with relations to support modalities. Goldblatt's "relational cover" semantics overcomes classical reasoning but introduces a new limitation: it relies upon a "modal localization" condition that restricts the class of models and complicates model construction. Goldblatt bypasses this restriction by using intricate order-theoretic completion arguments to prove completeness. In this article, we present a conservative extension of relational cover semantics that alleviates this restriction and is amenable to simpler and standard model construction techniques. We formalize our semantics in Agda and prove completeness constructively in the style of Normalization by Evaluation for a variety of IMLs featuring independent box and diamond modalities.
item.dc:creator: Nachiappan Valliappan

item.title: Formalizing Flag Algebras in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2607.23500v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Razborov's flag algebra method is one of the most successful tools for proving asymptotic density inequalities in extremal graph theory. It reduces an inequality about all large graphs avoiding a forbidden pattern to finitely many algebraic conditions, and a certificate satisfying them can be found by semidefinite programming. We formalize the method for finite simple graphs in Lean 4, building on Mathlib. The formalization covers flags and their densities, the flag algebra as a quotient vector space, positive homomorphisms as limits of graph sequences, Razborov's random extensions, and the downward operator that averages out labels. On top of this theory, we build verified computation of flag densities and a tactic that turns certificates found by semidefinite programming into Lean proofs. The certificate serves only as candidate data; Lean checks every fact the proof uses. With this development we verify seven Tur\'an-type upper bounds. Adding lower-bound constructions proved in Lean yields the asymptotic form of Mantel's theorem and the asymptotic Erd\H{o}s pentagon theorem $\pi(C_5;K_3)=24/625$; to our knowledge, the latter has not previously been formalized in a proof assistant. We also prove two inequalities of Goodman. All density theorems reported here depend only on the standard axioms of Lean's logic. Formalization also led us to treat forbidden subgraphs with a different semantics. Instead of building a separate flag algebra for each forbidden family, we keep a single algebra of all graphs and impose the constraint only when interpreting an inequality, through randomly labeled limits of graphs satisfying it. We prove that this ensemble semantics yields the intended density bounds, and that a condition we call root-plantability characterizes when it agrees with the standard semantics.
item.dc:creator: Gyeongwon Jeong, Seonghun Park, Jihoon Hyun, Sang-il Oum, Hongseok Yang

item.title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14738v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed. Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour. We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate. We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.
item.dc:creator: Ehud Shapiro
